description: AstroGuard AI combines computer science, AI, and human health to protect astronauts during space missions. We aim to build a health-monitoring system that analyzes data, detects unusual patterns, visualizes trends, and provides early alerts. We're looking for members interested in AI/ML, software, data science, biology, physiology, or space medicine.
summary:
AstroGuard AI is a working health-monitoring software prototype that helps astronauts recognize changes in their daily health indicators during long-duration missions. We developed a browser dashboard that tracks seven indicators, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, oxygen saturation, temperature, stress, and exercise.

The software compares readings with each crew member’s personal baseline, flags unusual or sustained changes, and explains the evidence behind each alert. Astronauts can add context, verify readings, record their review, and export an evidence packet for further discussion.

Our project addresses the challenge by connecting health information to a practical crew review process, especially when communication delays limit immediate support from Earth. NASA’s human research and sleep-risk resources informed the design. All demonstration health data are simulated, and the detector has not been validated on real astronaut data.

AstroGuard AI aims to make health changes easier to understand and discuss. It is a decision-support tool, not a diagnostic device.
details:
What we developed

AstroGuard AI is a browser-based health-monitoring prototype that helps astronauts review changes in their daily health indicators. It brings seven indicators into one dashboard: resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep duration, oxygen saturation, body temperature, perceived stress, and exercise completion.

Our goal was to give astronauts a useful starting point for understanding their readings and deciding what needs closer review, particularly when communication delays make immediate support from Earth difficult.

How it works

The software uses the first 14 days of readings to establish a personal baseline for each indicator. It estimates the median and variability, then compares subsequent readings against that baseline. This allows the system to highlight changes relative to the individual.

The prototype flags readings that cross developer-defined statistical thresholds. Three consecutive flags establish persistence for an indicator, and persistent changes across two or more indicators produce a combined review prompt. These settings illustrate the approach; they are not NASA-approved medical thresholds.

Each flag includes an explanation showing the current reading, baseline, and size of the deviation. Missing readings remain visibly unavailable. Astronauts can add context, follow a review checklist, record their review, and export an evidence packet. Recording a review does not automatically clear active flags.

Demonstration and technical checks

The website includes two synthetic crew profiles and four repeatable scenarios: stable readings, gradual fatigue, abrupt changes, and sensor dropout. It also supports importing a CSV containing 28 days of readings.

We developed a separate Python experiment covering 180 synthetic days. In that experiment, a gradual decline beginning on day 61 first produces a combined review prompt on day 76. This demonstrates the software’s response to constructed inputs; it does not establish clinical accuracy or warning time before illness.

All demonstration health readings are simulated. No real astronaut dataset trained or validated the detector.

Benefits and intended impact

AstroGuard AI aims to make daily health information easier for crews to interpret. Instead of presenting an unexplained alert, it shows what changed and preserves the evidence for discussion with a crew medical officer or later ground review.

Analysis runs locally in the browser without requiring an external AI inference service. This design explores how crews could review information with less dependence on continuous connectivity. The prototype does not include a live communications relay.

The intended impact is clearer, better-documented crew review. We have not yet measured improvements in health outcomes, decision quality, or review time. AstroGuard AI is a decision-support tool, not a diagnostic device.

Tools and development

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interface and statistical analysis, SVG for trend charts, browser storage for demonstration records, CSV import, and JSON evidence export. A service worker implements caching, although offline behavior still requires browser verification.

The separate experiment uses Python’s standard library to generate synthetic readings and export reproducible results. No dedicated hardware or live medical sensors were used. OpenAI ChatGPT assisted with implementation, synthetic data, testing, writing, and presentation materials.

NASA resources and creativity

NASA’s Human Research Program hazard framework and Human Research Roadmap sleep-risk evidence informed our focus on sleep, workload, and understandable crew review. These resources informed the design rather than supplying training data or medical thresholds.

The project’s creative contribution is the connection between personal baselines, explainable flags, and a crew review record. The sensor-dropout scenario also makes uncertainty visible: unavailable information never becomes a reassuring result.

Factors we considered and next steps

We considered individual differences, interacting signals, missing measurements, communication delays, and the need to keep explanations understandable. We also considered the limits of the available indicators. The prototype does not directly measure radiation exposure, bone loss, immune function, or behavioral illness.

Next steps include sensor-quality and timestamp checks, baseline review across mission phases, and evaluation with suitable analog-mission data and domain experts. We would measure false alerts, missed changes, and crew review time, alongside privacy, security, and usability testing, before considering operational use.
